questions.q: Monitoring vs observability: what is the actual difference, and what does each telemetry signal (metrics, logs, traces, profiles) let you answer?
questions.a:
### Monitoring
Watching **known** failure modes with predefined checks and dashboards: "is CPU above 80%?", "is the error rate above 1%?". Answers questions you anticipated.

### Observability
The ability to answer **new** questions about system behaviour from its outputs without shipping new code: "why are payments from one merchant in one region slow since 14:05?". Requires rich, correlated, high-dimensional telemetry.

### Signals
| Signal | Shape | Best for | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Metrics** | numeric time series with labels | trends, alerting, SLOs, cheap at scale | low cardinality only; no per-request detail |
| **Logs** | timestamped events, ideally structured | detailed context of discrete events, audit | volume and cost; hard to correlate without ids |
| **Traces** | causally linked spans across services | latency breakdown, dependency paths, where time goes | sampling; instrumentation coverage |
| **Profiles** | CPU, allocation, lock samples | which code consumes resources | overhead, tooling maturity |
| **Events** (deploys, flags, config) | change markers | correlating changes with symptoms | often forgotten |

### Correlation is the point
Trace id in logs, exemplars on metrics, deploy markers on dashboards: jump from an alert (metric) to an example request (trace) to its details (logs) to the hot code (profile).

  DP[Deploy marker 14:02] -.correlate.-> AL
pts: Monitoring checks known failures; observability answers new questions.
Metrics: trends and alerts; logs: event detail; traces: causality and latency.

Change events explain many incidents.

questions.q: Explain counters, gauges, up-down counters and histograms. Instrument a .NET service with System.Diagnostics.Metrics correctly, including units and labels.
questions.a:
### Instrument types
| Type | Semantics | Example | Query |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Counter** | monotonically increasing | requests, payments created, bytes sent | rate over time |
| **UpDownCounter** | can go up and down, summed | items in a queue, active connections | current value |
| **Gauge** (observable) | sampled current value | memory used, pool size, temperature | last value |
| **Histogram** | distribution of measurements | request duration, payload size | percentiles, averages, counts |

### Rules
- **Durations as histograms**, never as averages or gauges; percentiles can't be averaged across instances, histograms can be aggregated.
- Units in names or metadata (seconds for durations per OpenTelemetry conventions, bytes for sizes).
- **Low-cardinality labels** only: route template, status class, scheme, region. Never user id, payment id, raw URL.
- Prefer semantic convention names ({{http.server.request.duration}}) where they exist.
- Create instruments once (static or via IMeterFactory), not per request.
pts: Counter, up-down counter, gauge, histogram.
Durations as histograms.
Units and semantic convention names.
Low-cardinality labels only.
Create instruments once via IMeterFactory.

questions.q: What makes logging "structured", and how do you log correctly in .NET (message templates, levels, scopes, high-performance logging)?
questions.a:
### Structured logging
Each log entry is an event with **named properties** (PaymentId, Amount, Merchant) plus the rendered message, emitted as JSON or OTLP. Backends index properties, so you query {{PaymentId = 'P-1'}} instead of grepping text.

### .NET rules
- **Message templates** with placeholders, not string interpolation: {{LogInformation("Payment {PaymentId} created", id)}} keeps PaymentId as a property; {{$"..."}} interpolation destroys structure and allocates even when the level is disabled.
- **Levels** meaningfully: Error (needs attention), Warning (unexpected but handled), Information (business events, low volume), Debug/Trace (development; off in production by default).
- **Scopes** to attach context (tenant, correlation) to all logs in a block.
- **LoggerMessage source generator** for hot paths: zero-allocation, compile-time templates.
- **Trace correlation**: with OpenTelemetry, TraceId and SpanId are attached automatically.

### What not to log
Secrets, tokens, full card numbers, passwords, entire request bodies, PII beyond what is justified.
pts: Named properties, not text blobs.
Message templates, never interpolation.
Meaningful levels; Debug off in production.
Scopes for context; source-generated logging for hot paths.
No secrets or unnecessary PII.

questions.q: How does distributed tracing work: spans, parent-child relationships, W3C trace context, and what breaks propagation?
questions.a:
### Concepts
- **Trace**: one end-to-end operation (a payment request), identified by a 16-byte trace id.
- **Span**: a timed operation within it (HTTP server, DB call, outbound HTTP), with span id, parent span id, attributes, events, status, kind (server, client, producer, consumer, internal).
- **Context propagation**: the current trace and span ids travel with calls so the next service creates child spans.

### W3C Trace Context
{{traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<parent-span-id>-<flags>}} (flags include sampled), plus {{tracestate}} for vendor data and **baggage** for user-defined key-values (use sparingly; it travels everywhere).

### In .NET
{{Activity}} is the span; ASP.NET Core and HttpClient instrumentation read and write {{traceparent}} automatically; {{ActivitySource}} creates custom spans.

### What breaks propagation
| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| async messaging without headers | inject context into message headers, extract in consumers |
| thread pool work started without flowing context (custom threads) | use async APIs; ExecutionContext flows by default |
| proxies or gateways stripping headers | allow traceparent through |
| uninstrumented libraries or languages | instrument or use auto-instrumentation |
| background jobs | start new traces linked to the originating trace |

questions.q: Compare the RED method, the USE method and Google's four golden signals. Which do you apply to services vs infrastructure, and what do they miss?
questions.a:
| Method | Signals | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **RED** | Rate, Errors, Duration | request-driven services (APIs, consumers) |
| **USE** | Utilisation, Saturation, Errors | resources: CPU, memory, disks, connection pools, thread pools, queues |
| **Golden signals** | Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation | user-facing systems: RED plus saturation |

### Applying them
- Every API endpoint and consumer: RED, with duration as histograms and errors split by type (4xx client vs 5xx server, timeouts).
- Every bounded resource: USE (DB connection pool in use vs max, thread pool queue length, Kafka consumer lag as saturation).
- Dashboards top-down: golden signals per service, then drill into USE for its resources.

### What they miss
- **Correctness**: a service can be fast and error-free while computing wrong fees.
- **Business outcomes**: payment success rate, approval rate, settlement completeness.
- **Freshness** for data pipelines (age of the newest processed record).
- **Dependencies' contribution** (needs traces).
Add business and correctness signals for critical flows.

questions.q: Explain the OpenTelemetry architecture: API, SDK, instrumentation libraries, OTLP, the Collector. Why is vendor neutrality valuable in practice?
questions.a:
### Components
| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **API** | what code calls (in .NET: System.Diagnostics Activity, Meter, ILogger) |
| **SDK** | implementation: sampling, processors, batching, resource attributes, exporters |
| **Instrumentation libraries** | ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, SqlClient, EF Core, gRPC, Kafka, Redis |
| **Semantic conventions** | standard attribute and metric names ({{http.request.method}}, {{db.system}}, {{service.name}}) |
| **OTLP** | the wire protocol (gRPC or HTTP) for traces, metrics, logs |
| **Collector** | receives, processes (batch, filter, redact, sample, enrich) and exports to one or more backends |

### Deployment patterns
Apps export OTLP to a **local agent** collector (sidecar or DaemonSet) which forwards to a **gateway** collector tier that does tail sampling, redaction, routing and export.

### Vendor neutrality in practice
- Switch or split backends (Datadog to Grafana, or both during migration) by changing collector config, not app code.
- Consistent naming across languages and teams.
- Negotiating leverage on cost.
- One instrumentation investment reused for years.

questions.q: Instrument an ASP.NET Core service end to end: what to enable, which attributes to add, what to filter out, and how to avoid overhead.
questions.a:
### Enable
ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, SqlClient or EF Core, gRPC client, Redis, Kafka (via Confluent instrumentation or manual), runtime metrics, process metrics, plus custom ActivitySource and Meter for domain operations.

### Enrich
- Resource: {{service.name}}, version, environment, region, Kubernetes pod and node.
- Spans: route template (automatic), tenant or channel (low cardinality), domain outcomes (payment decision).
- Logs: scopes for tenant and correlation; TraceId automatic.

### Filter
- Health and readiness endpoints, metrics scraping, static files: drop from traces.
- SQL statement text only if sanitised (no literals with PII); keep {{db.operation}} and table.
- Request and response bodies: never by default.

### Overhead
Batch exporters (async), sampling for traces, LoggerMessage for logs, avoid creating spans for tiny in-process operations, cap attribute counts. Measure overhead in performance tests (typically low single-digit percent).

Enrich with resource and low-cardinality domain attributes.
Filter health checks; no raw SQL or bodies.
Batch exporters and sampling.
Measure overhead.

questions.q: Design OpenTelemetry Collector pipelines: receivers, processors, exporters, and the agent and gateway tiers. What processing belongs where?
questions.a:
### Pipeline anatomy
{{receivers -> processors -> exporters}} per signal type (traces, metrics, logs), plus **connectors** that bridge pipelines (spanmetrics creates RED metrics from spans).

### Agent tier (per node or sidecar)
- Receives OTLP from local apps; scrapes local endpoints (kubelet, host metrics).
- **k8sattributes** processor to add pod, namespace, node labels.
- **memory_limiter** and **batch**.
- Forwards to gateway; small buffers.

### Gateway tier (horizontally scaled)
- **tail_sampling** (needs all spans of a trace on the same instance: use the **loadbalancing exporter** in the agent keyed by trace id).
- **Redaction** (attributes, transform with OTTL) for PII.
- **Filter** to drop noisy data.
- Routing to multiple backends, retries with persistent queues.

### Operational concerns
Backpressure (memory limiter refuses data before OOM), persistent queues for exporter outages, monitoring the collector itself (its own metrics), and config as code with validation.
pts: Receivers, processors, exporters, connectors per signal.
Agent: k8s enrichment, batching, forwarding.
Gateway: tail sampling, redaction, routing.
Load-balance by trace id for tail sampling.
Memory limiter, persistent queues, self-monitoring.
questions.ex: A single gateway collector without memory limits OOM-crashed during an incident spike, losing the very traces needed. A scaled gateway tier with memory_limiter, persistent queues and trace-id load balancing kept telemetry flowing through the next incident.

questions.q: What is metric cardinality, why does it explode, and how do you prevent and fix it?
questions.a:
### Definition
The number of unique time series = combinations of metric name and label values. {{http_requests_total}} with labels route (50) x status (10) x pod (40) = 20,000 series. Add {{customer_id}} (1M) and you have 20 billion: the backend falls over or the bill explodes.

### Common causes
- IDs as labels (user, payment, order, trace id).
- Raw URL paths instead of route templates ({{/accounts/123}}).
- Error messages or exception text as labels.
- Unbounded enums (free-text merchant names).
- Pod and container ids multiplied across many metrics with frequent restarts.

### Prevention
- Label allow-lists in code reviews and the collector (drop or aggregate unknown labels).
- Route templates only; bucket numeric values (amount bands).
- High-cardinality questions belong in **traces or logs** (query by payment id there).
- Cardinality budgets per service with alerts on series growth.

### Fixing
Find top series contributors (backend cardinality explorer, {{topk}} by label count), drop labels at the collector, deploy code fixes.

      - { key: url.full, action: delete }

        - 'attributes["http.route"] == nil and metric.name == "http.server.request.duration"'   # drop unrouted noise
---

# topk(10, count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".+"}))

~~~

questions.q: How do you keep PII, secrets and card data out of logs and traces across many services? Design layered redaction.
questions.a:
### Layers
1. **Don't emit**: log identifiers (customer id) rather than names, emails, card numbers; never log tokens, passwords, bodies.
2. **Type-level protection**: data classification attributes on properties ({{[PersonalData]}}, {{[SensitiveData]}}) with **Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction** redactors applied by the logging pipeline.
3. **Framework defaults**: no request/response body logging; header allow-lists for HTTP logging.
4. **Collector redaction**: OTTL transform or redaction processor masking patterns (PAN-like numbers, emails, IBANs) as a safety net.
5. **Backend controls**: access control, retention by data class, field-level masking in UI.

### Verification
Automated scans of log samples for PII patterns (PAN with Luhn check, emails, national ids) with alerts; tests that sensitive types render redacted.

### Erasure
If PII does land in logs, retention policies and the ability to delete by subject matter (GDPR). Short retention for debug-level data.
pts: Don't emit sensitive data in the first place.
Classify types and redact in the logging pipeline.
Collector pattern redaction as a safety net.
Scan log samples for PII automatically.
Retention and access controls by data class.

questions.q: Head sampling vs tail sampling: how does each work, what does each cost, and which strategy would you choose for a payments platform?
questions.a:
### Head sampling
The decision is made at the **start** of a trace (root span), usually probabilistic by trace id, and propagated (sampled flag in traceparent) so downstream services follow it ({{ParentBased}}).
- Cheap, no buffering.
- Blind: a 1% sample keeps 1% of errors and slow requests too.

### Tail sampling
Spans are buffered (in a collector gateway) until the trace completes, then policies decide: keep all errors, all slow traces, specific tenants or routes, plus a small baseline percentage.
- Keeps the interesting traces.
- Costs memory and CPU in collectors; requires all spans of a trace to reach the same collector instance (trace-id load balancing); decision wait adds delay; very long traces complicate it.

### Payments strategy
- Apps: parent-based head sampling at a **high rate** (or 100%) to the collector, so tail sampling has data.
- Gateway: tail sampling keeping 100% errors, 100% above the latency SLO threshold, 100% for flagged debug tenants, 5 to 10% baseline.
- Metrics computed **before** sampling (spanmetrics connector or app metrics), so RED numbers stay exact.
- Logs keep trace ids even for unsampled traces (useful for search).
pts: Head: decided at root, cheap, blind to outcome.
Tail: decided after completion, keeps errors and slow traces.
Tail needs trace-id affinity and buffering.
Compute metrics before sampling.
Combine high head rate with tail policies.
questions.ex: At 1% head sampling, a payments team had no trace for any of the 40 failed payments a customer complained about. Tail sampling keeping all errors and slow traces with a 5% baseline cost 30% less than 10% head sampling and always had the failing traces.

questions.q: How do you correlate signals in practice: trace ids in logs, exemplars on histograms, and links from dashboards to traces?
questions.a:
### Mechanisms
| Link | How |
|---|---|
| **Logs to traces** | logs carry TraceId and SpanId (automatic with OpenTelemetry logging in .NET); log UI links to trace view |
| **Metrics to traces** | **exemplars**: a histogram bucket stores a sample trace id of a request that fell in it; clicking a latency spike opens an actual slow trace |
| **Traces to logs** | trace view queries logs by trace id |
| **Traces to profiles** | span profiles: profiler samples tagged with span ids |
| **Everything to changes** | deploy and flag-change annotations on dashboards |
| **Users to traces** | return trace id in a response header ({{traceresponse}} or {{X-Request-Id}}) and show it in error pages for support |

### Requirements
Same {{service.name}} and resource attributes across signals, consistent time sync, sampling decisions compatible with exemplars (exemplar traces should be kept: tail-sample traces referenced by exemplars or keep slow ones anyway), and backends that support the links (Grafana with Prometheus/Mimir exemplars, Tempo, Loki; most vendors).

Exemplars connect metric spikes to real traces.
Deploy and flag annotations explain changes.

questions.q: Define SLIs and SLOs for a payments API and a statement-generation batch job. What makes a good SLI?
questions.a:
### Good SLIs
- Measure what **users experience** (at the edge or client), not internal resources.
- Expressed as a **ratio of good events to valid events**.
- Precise definitions: which requests count, what "good" means (status and latency), measurement point.

### Payments API
| SLI | Definition | SLO (28 days) |
|---|---|---|
| Availability | non-5xx responses / all valid requests (excluding 4xx client errors) at the gateway | 99.95% |
| Latency | requests completed under 500 ms / all successful requests | 99% |
| Correctness (business) | payments settled with matching amount and fee / payments settled | 99.999% |

### Statement batch job
| SLI | Definition | SLO |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | statements available by 06:00 local / statements due | 99.5% of days |
| Completeness | accounts with a generated statement / accounts eligible | 100% (any gap pages) |
| Correctness | statements passing reconciliation checks / generated | 99.99% |

### Choosing targets
From user needs and history, not "five nines" by default; each extra nine multiplies cost. SLOs are agreed with product and business owners.

~~~yaml
# SLO as code (OpenSLO-style)
apiVersion: openslo/v1
kind: SLO
metadata: { name: payments-api-availability }
spec:
  service: payments-api
  budgetingMethod: Occurrences
  timeWindow: [{ duration: 28d, isRolling: true }]
  objectives: [{ target: 0.9995 }]
  indicator:
    metadata: { name: gateway-availability }
    spec:
      ratioMetric:
        good:  { metricSource: { type: Prometheus, spec: { query: 'sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*", code!~"5.."}[5m]))' } } }
        total: { metricSource: { type: Prometheus, spec: { query: 'sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*", code!~"4.."}[5m]))' } } }
~~~

Precise definitions and measurement points.
Include latency and correctness, not just availability.
Batch jobs: freshness, completeness, correctness.
Targets agreed with business; nines are expensive.

questions.q: What is an error budget, how do you compute it, and what should an error budget policy say when it is exhausted?
questions.a:
### Budget
Error budget = 1 minus SLO over the window. At 99.95% over 28 days: 0.05% of requests may fail, or about 20 minutes of full unavailability equivalent.

### Burn
Burn rate = observed error ratio / budget ratio. A burn rate of 1 consumes exactly the budget in the window; 14.4 consumes 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour.

### Policy (agreed in advance with product and engineering leadership)
| Budget state | Action |
|---|---|
| healthy (over 50% left) | normal feature work, normal deploy cadence |
| low (under 25%) | prioritise reliability items; extra review for risky changes |
| exhausted | freeze non-critical feature releases for the service (security and reliability fixes allowed) until budget recovers or a postmortem plan is accepted |
| repeated exhaustion | reliability engineering investment, revisit architecture or SLO |

### Why it works
It converts reliability debates into data: product can choose to spend budget on speed, but not unboundedly. It also protects teams: if the budget is healthy, there's no reason to slow down.

### Pitfalls
Policies nobody enforces, SLOs set too high to ever meet, budgets consumed by a dependency (decide how to attribute).

questions.q: Design alerting that pages humans only for real user impact. Explain symptom-based alerts and multi-window, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts.
questions.a:
### Principles
- **Page on symptoms** (users affected: SLO burn), not causes (CPU high, pod restarted). Causes go to dashboards or tickets.
- Every page must be **actionable**, urgent and have a runbook.
- Measure alert quality: pages per week, false positive rate, time to acknowledge.

### Multi-window, multi-burn-rate
Alert when the budget burns fast enough to matter, confirmed by a short window to reset quickly:
| Severity | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget consumed if sustained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| page | 1 h | 5 min | 14.4 | 2% in 1 h |
| page | 6 h | 30 min | 6 | 5% in 6 h |
| ticket | 3 d | 6 h | 1 | 10% in 3 d |
Both windows must exceed the threshold, which avoids flapping and detects both fast and slow burns.

### Other good alerts
Synthetic journey failures, dead-man's switches (no data or heartbeat missing), batch freshness breaches, certificate expiry well ahead.

~~~yaml
groups:
- name: payments-slo
  rules:
  - record: payments:error_ratio:rate5m
    expr: 1 - sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*",code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*",code!~"4.."}[5m]))
  - record: payments:error_ratio:rate1h
    expr: 1 - sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*",code!~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*",code!~"4.."}[1h]))
  - alert: PaymentsFastBurn
    expr: payments:error_ratio:rate1h > (14.4 * 0.0005) and payments:error_ratio:rate5m > (14.4 * 0.0005)
    labels: { severity: page, team: payments }
    annotations:
      summary: "Payments availability SLO burning fast (2% of budget per hour)"
      runbook: "https://runbooks.bank/payments/availability"
      dashboard: "https://grafana.bank/d/payments-slo"
~~~
pts: Page on symptoms, not causes.
Every page actionable with a runbook.
Multi-window multi-burn-rate catches fast and slow burns.
Short windows reset alerts quickly.
Dead-man's switches and synthetic checks.
questions.ex: An on-call rotation received 180 pages a week, mostly CPU and pod restart alerts; people ignored them and missed a real outage. Replacing them with SLO burn-rate alerts reduced pages to 6 a week, each meaningful, and time to acknowledge fell from 25 minutes to 3.

questions.q: How do you trace asynchronous flows through Kafka or Service Bus? Parent-child or links, and how do you measure end-to-end latency?
questions.a:
### Propagation
- Producer injects the current context into **message headers** ({{traceparent}}) when publishing; with an outbox, store the context in the outbox row so the relay publishes it.
- Consumer extracts it and starts a **consumer span**.

### Parent or link
| Choice | When |
|---|---|
| child of producer span | one message, one consumer; you want one trace per business flow |
| **span link** | batch consumers processing many messages (one span links to many producer contexts), fan-out to many consumers, long delays (hours) |
OpenTelemetry messaging conventions recommend links for batch receive and allow parent for single-message processing.

### Measuring end-to-end latency
- Producer timestamp in headers; consumer records {{now - produced_at}} as a histogram (queue latency), separate from processing time.
- Consumer lag (offsets behind) as a saturation metric.
- For business flows (payment initiated to posted), a metric computed at the final step using the original timestamp carried in the event.
pts: Inject context into message headers; outbox stores it.
Parent for single messages, links for batches and fan-out.
Measure queue latency separately from processing.
Consumer lag as saturation.
Business end-to-end latency from original timestamps.

questions.q: How do you observe Angular or React applications in production (real user monitoring), and connect frontend experience to backend traces?
questions.a:
### What to measure
- **Core Web Vitals**: LCP (loading), INP (interactivity), CLS (layout stability), plus TTFB.
- **JavaScript errors** with source maps (uploaded privately, not served publicly).
- **API calls** from the browser: latency and errors per endpoint as the user saw them.
- **User journeys**: login, payment submission, statement download: success rate and duration.
- Release and feature-flag version per session.

### Connecting to backend
- OpenTelemetry JS (web) instruments fetch/XHR and injects {{traceparent}} so backend spans join the browser span; CORS must allow the header ({{Access-Control-Allow-Headers}}).
- Session id attribute to group a user's journey (not a personal identifier).

### Privacy and cost
No PII in attributes (mask inputs in session replay or disable it for banking screens), sample sessions, respect consent banners where required, and keep RUM data in the right region.

### SLOs
Journey-level SLOs ("payment submission succeeded within 3 seconds as seen by the browser") capture what users feel better than server-side metrics.

questions.q: What makes a dashboard useful during an incident? Design the dashboard hierarchy for a payments domain.
questions.a:
### Principles
- **Answer a question** per dashboard ("is payments healthy?", "why is this service slow?"), not "every metric we have".
- Top-down: user impact first (SLOs, journeys), then service golden signals, then resources and dependencies.
- Consistent layout across services so on-call engineers aren't relearning.
- Annotations for deploys, flag changes and incidents.
- Links to traces (exemplars), logs and runbooks.
- Units, thresholds and SLO lines visible; avoid averages for latency.

### Hierarchy
| Level | Contents |
|---|---|
| 1. Domain overview | journey SLOs (initiate, authorise, settle), error budgets, business KPIs (payments per minute, success rate by scheme) |
| 2. Service dashboards (templated) | RED per route, dependencies' RED, saturation (pools, threads, lag), deploy markers |
| 3. Resource dashboards | database (query latency, waits, locks), Kafka (lag per group), Kubernetes (pods, throttling) |
| 4. Debug views | ad hoc exploration in the query tool, not permanent dashboards |

### Dashboards as code
Generated from templates (Grafana Jsonnet/Grafonnet, Terraform providers) per service, so new services get the standard set automatically.

Consistent templated layouts.

questions.q: Log ingestion costs have doubled. Design a log pipeline that controls cost while keeping what you need for incidents, security and audit.
questions.a:
### Understand the volume
Top emitters by service, level and message template (event id). Usually 10 templates produce most of the volume: health checks, per-request debug logs, verbose framework logs, retry loops.

### Controls
| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| Fix at source: levels, remove per-request info logs that duplicate traces | largest saving |
| Drop at collector: health checks, known noise by event id | immediate |
| **Sampling** of high-volume informational logs (keep all warnings and errors) | proportional saving |
| **Tiering**: hot searchable store for 7 to 14 days, cheap object storage (Parquet) for months, rehydrate on demand | storage cost |
| **Routing by purpose**: security and audit logs to the SIEM and immutable store with legal retention; operational logs to the observability backend | right cost per purpose |
| Convert logs to metrics where you only count them | cheap |
| Per-team budgets and showback | accountability |

### Keep
Errors and warnings with context, audit events (separate pipeline, never sampled), security events, and logs correlated by trace id for sampled traces.

processors:
  filter/noise:
    logs:
      log_record:
        - 'attributes["url.path"] == "/health/ready"'
        - 'attributes["event.id"] == 2001 and severity_number < SEVERITY_NUMBER_WARN'    # per-request info log duplicated by traces
  probabilistic_sampler/info:
    sampling_percentage: 10
    attribute_source: record
    from_attribute: trace_id           # keep logs consistent with trace decisions where possible
  routing:
    default_exporters: [otlphttp/loki]
    table:
      - { statement: 'route() where attributes["log.category"] == "audit"', exporters: [otlphttp/audit-worm] }
      - { statement: 'route() where attributes["log.category"] == "security"', exporters: [otlphttp/siem] }
service:
  pipelines:
    logs/ops:      { receivers: [otlp], processors: [memory_limiter, filter/noise, batch], exporters: [routing] }
~~~

Fix at source, drop noise at collector.
Sample info logs; keep warnings and errors.
Tier storage and route by purpose.
Audit logs on a separate unsampled pipeline.
questions.ex: A bank's log bill hit 2.1M a year; 62% came from 8 message templates, mostly per-request info logs duplicating traces and health checks. Removing and sampling them, plus 14-day hot retention with Parquet archives, cut cost by 58% with no incident-impacting gaps.

questions.q: A .NET service has high latency but low CPU. Walk through a systematic investigation in production.
questions.a:
### Low CPU plus high latency means waiting
Something is blocking: I/O, locks, thread pool starvation, connection pools, GC pauses, or a slow dependency.

### Steps
1. **Traces**: where does the time go? A slow dependency span (database, HTTP, Redis) or gaps between spans (in-process waiting).
2. **Thread pool**: {{dotnet-counters}} for {{threadpool-queue-length}}, {{threadpool-thread-count}} growing slowly (starvation from sync-over-async: {{.Result}}, {{.Wait()}}, sync I/O).
3. **Connection pools**: SqlClient pool in use vs max, HttpClient connections per server, Redis multiplexer timeouts; pool exhaustion queues requests.
4. **Locks and contention**: {{monitor-lock-contention-count}}; a {{lock}} around I/O.
5. **GC**: time in GC, gen2 collections, LOH allocations; pauses from large allocations.
6. **Dependency side**: database waits (Query Store, wait stats), downstream service latency.
7. **Capture**: {{dotnet-trace}} (with thread time / wait analysis) or a dump ({{dotnet-dump}}) and {{clrstack}} across threads to see what threads are blocked on.

### Typical fixes
Remove sync-over-async, size or fix pools, add timeouts, move I/O out of locks, reduce allocations, fix slow queries.
questions.code:
~~~bash
# Attach to the pod (dotnet-monitor sidecar or ephemeral debug container with tools)
kubectl debug -it payments-api-7c9f -n payments --image=mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:9.0 --target=app -- bash
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-counters dotnet-trace dotnet-dump && export PATH="$PATH:/root/.dotnet/tools"

dotnet-counters monitor -p 1 --counters System.Runtime,Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting,System.Net.Http
#   threadpool-queue-length rising, threadpool-thread-count creeping up by ~1/s  -> starvation
dotnet-trace collect -p 1 --profile cpu-sampling --duration 00:00:30 -o slow.nettrace
dotnet-dump collect -p 1 -o hang.dmp
dotnet-dump analyze hang.dmp -c "clrstack -all" | grep -B2 -A8 "Task.Wait\|GetResult\|Monitor.Enter" | head -80
~~~
pts: Low CPU with high latency means waiting.
Traces locate slow dependencies or in-process gaps.
Check thread pool, connection pools, locks, GC.
Capture traces or dumps to see blocked threads.
Fix sync-over-async, pools, locks, queries.

questions.q: Pods of a .NET service are OOM-killed every few hours. How do you confirm a memory leak, find its root cause, and distinguish it from normal GC behaviour?
questions.a:
### Leak or not?
- Normal: memory grows to a plateau set by GC heuristics and container limits (Server GC uses more memory; it respects {{DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit}} or container limits).
- Leak: **gen2 heap size after full GCs keeps rising** over hours, or native memory grows (unmanaged allocations, handles).

### Signals
{{dotnet-counters}}: gc-heap-size, gen-2-gc-count, loh-size, poh-size, working set, alloc rate. Container memory vs managed heap: a big gap suggests native memory (unmanaged libraries, thread stacks, memory-mapped files).

### Find the cause
1. **gcdump** at two points in time ({{dotnet-gcdump}}), compare object counts and retained sizes: which types grow?
2. **Full dump** ({{dotnet-dump}}) for {{dumpheap -stat}}, {{gcroot}} to find what keeps objects alive.
3. Common culprits: static caches without eviction (unbounded {{ConcurrentDictionary}}), event handlers never unsubscribed, {{IMemoryCache}} without size limits, HttpClient created per request (sockets and handlers), captured closures in timers, EF Core DbContext held as singleton, large {{MemoryStream}} buffers kept, logging scopes captured.

### Mitigate while fixing
Memory limits with headroom, {{GCHeapHardLimitPercent}}, restart policies, and an alert on gen2 heap trend before OOM.
questions.code:
~~~bash
# Two gcdumps 30 minutes apart, compare growth
dotnet-gcdump collect -p 1 -o t0.gcdump
sleep 1800
dotnet-gcdump collect -p 1 -o t1.gcdump
dotnet-gcdump report t1.gcdump | head -30          # top types by size; compare with t0

# Full dump analysis for roots
dotnet-dump collect -p 1 --type Heap -o heap.dmp
dotnet-dump analyze heap.dmp -c "dumpheap -stat" | tail -20
dotnet-dump analyze heap.dmp -c "dumpheap -type Bank.Payments.QuoteCacheEntry -short" | head -3
dotnet-dump analyze heap.dmp -c "gcroot 00007f3a2c1d4e80"     # who keeps it alive? (e.g. static QuoteCache._entries)
~~~
pts: Plateau is normal; rising gen2 after full GCs is a leak.
Compare managed heap with container memory for native leaks.
gcdump diffs show growing types; dumps show roots.
Usual suspects: unbounded caches, handlers, per-request HttpClient.
Alert on gen2 trend; set heap limits.
questions.ex: A quote service's static dictionary cached quotes by request id with no eviction; it grew 400 MB per hour. A gcdump diff showed QuoteCacheEntry dominating, gcroot pointed to the static field, and replacing it with a size-limited MemoryCache stopped the OOM kills.

questions.q: How do you make .NET diagnostics (traces, dumps, counters) available in Kubernetes production safely, including automatic capture when problems occur?
questions.a:
### dotnet-monitor
A sidecar (or ambient tool) that connects to the app's diagnostic port and exposes an authenticated HTTP API to collect traces, dumps, gcdumps, logs and metrics on demand.

### Collection rules (automatic capture)
Triggers such as high CPU for N seconds, thread pool queue length above a threshold, request duration above X, or GC heap size; actions collect a trace or dump and upload it to blob storage.

### Safety
| Concern | Control |
|---|---|
| Access | API authentication (API key or Azure AD), network policy so only operators reach it |
| PII in dumps | dumps contain memory, treat as sensitive data: encrypted storage, restricted access, short retention |
| Overhead | limit concurrent collections, trace profiles with low overhead, dumps only on triggers with cooldowns |
| Disk | write to shared or ephemeral storage with limits; upload and delete |

### Alternatives
Ephemeral debug containers with dotnet tools, Azure Monitor profiler and snapshot debugger, continuous profilers (Pyroscope, Datadog) for always-on CPU and allocation profiles.
pts: dotnet-monitor exposes diagnostics via an authenticated API.
Collection rules capture dumps and traces automatically.
Dumps are sensitive data: encrypt, restrict, expire.
Limit overhead with cooldowns and action limits.
Continuous profilers for always-on insight.
questions.ex: Intermittent 10-second stalls happened at night and vanished before anyone could attach tools. A dotnet-monitor rule on thread pool queue length captured a dump during the next stall, revealing a sync database call inside a timer callback.

questions.q: Traces show the database span is slow. How do you go from the span to the root cause in SQL Server or PostgreSQL, and what database telemetry should be in place?
questions.a:
### From span to query
- DB client spans carry {{db.system}}, {{db.operation}}, {{db.collection.name}} (table) and optionally sanitised statement text. Add a **query tag** (comment with route or operation name) so DBAs can map queries to code.
- EF Core: {{TagWith}} adds comments visible in Query Store and Extended Events.

### Database-side telemetry
| SQL Server | PostgreSQL | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| Query Store | pg_stat_statements, auto_explain | top queries by duration, CPU, reads; plan changes over time |
| Wait statistics ({{sys.dm_os_wait_stats}}, per-query waits in Query Store) | pg_stat_activity wait events | where time goes: locks, I/O, CPU, memory grants |
| Blocking and deadlocks (Extended Events, blocked process report) | pg_locks, log_lock_waits | contention |
| Index usage, missing indexes | pg_stat_user_indexes | design issues |
| Connection pool metrics from the app | same | pool exhaustion vs DB slowness |

### Typical root causes
Plan regression after statistics update or parameter sniffing, missing index, lock contention from long transactions, N+1 queries (many fast spans), memory grant waits, log write latency.
questions.code:
~~~csharp
// Tag queries so database tools map them back to code paths
var rows = await db.Payments
    .TagWith("payments-api:GET /merchants/{id}/payments")          // appears as a comment in Query Store
    .Where(p => p.MerchantId == merchantId && p.CreatedAt >= from)
    .OrderByDescending(p => p.CreatedAt)
    .Take(50)
    .AsNoTracking()
    .ToListAsync(ct);
~~~
~~~sql
-- SQL Server: find regressed queries for that tag in Query Store (last 24h vs previous week)
SELECT TOP 10 q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text, rs.avg_duration / 1000.0 AS avg_ms, rs.count_executions, p.plan_id
FROM sys.query_store_query q
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON p.query_id = q.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval i ON i.runtime_stats_interval_id = rs.runtime_stats_interval_id
WHERE qt.query_sql_text LIKE '%payments-api:GET /merchants%' AND i.start_time > DATEADD(hour, -24, SYSUTCDATETIME())
ORDER BY rs.avg_duration DESC;
~~~
pts: Tag queries with route or operation names.
Query Store or pg_stat_statements for top and regressed queries.
Wait statistics show where time goes.
Blocking, deadlock and index telemetry.
Distinguish pool exhaustion from DB slowness.
questions.ex: Merchant payment listing p99 jumped from 120 ms to 4 s after a statistics update; Query Store showed a new plan with a scan. Forcing the previous plan restored latency immediately, and a covering index removed the dependency on plan luck.

questions.q: Describe a mature incident response process: severity levels, roles, communication cadence, and the first 15 minutes of a major incident.
questions.a:
### Severity
| Sev | Definition (example) |
|---|---|
| SEV1 | critical journey down or data integrity at risk for many customers (payments failing) |
| SEV2 | significant degradation or partial outage |
| SEV3 | minor impact, workaround exists |
Severity drives who joins, communication cadence and regulator notification checks.

### Roles
- **Incident commander (IC)**: coordinates, decides, keeps the timeline; does not debug.
- **Operations lead(s)**: investigate and mitigate.
- **Communications lead**: internal and customer updates, status page, regulator liaison when needed.
- **Scribe**: timeline and decisions.
- Subject matter experts paged as needed.

### First 15 minutes
1. Acknowledge, declare severity, open the incident channel and bridge.
2. Assign IC and comms.
3. Establish impact (which journeys, customers, regions) from SLO dashboards.
4. Check recent changes (deploys, flags, config, infrastructure) and **mitigate first**: roll back, flag off, fail over, shed load.
5. First update to stakeholders with impact, mitigation in progress, next update time.

### Principles
Mitigate before root-causing, communicate on a fixed cadence (for example every 30 minutes for SEV1), and hand over explicitly when tired.

questions.q: What makes a postmortem useful rather than ritual? Structure it and describe how to make action items actually happen.
questions.a:
### Blameless, systems-focused
Assume people acted reasonably with the information and tools they had; ask what made the failure possible and what made detection and recovery slow. Blame stops people from sharing the truth.

### Structure
1. Summary: what happened, impact (customers, duration, money, regulatory), severity.
2. Timeline: detection, escalation, mitigation, resolution, with evidence links.
3. Contributing factors (usually several): technical, process, organisational. Avoid a single "root cause" narrative.
4. What went well (keep doing it).
5. Where we got lucky.
6. Action items: specific, owned, dated, prioritised; classified as prevent, detect, mitigate.
7. Lessons and follow-up questions.

### Making actions happen
- Track action items in the team backlog with a postmortem label; review completion weekly in an operations review.
- Limit to a handful of high-value actions rather than 25 vague ones.
- Senior leadership reviews SEV1 postmortems and unblocks cross-team actions.
- Measure action completion rate and repeat incidents.

### Share
Publish internally; a searchable library of postmortems; periodic themes analysis (recurring causes).

| 2 | Prevent | Flag rollouts above 25% require canary-style analysis window | platform-flags | 2026-11-10 | open |
| 3 | Mitigate | Runbook: one-click flag rollback from incident bot | team-sre | 2026-10-20 | open |
| 4 | Prevent | Contract test for fraud-scoring-v2 response schema with card-auth | team-fraud | 2026-10-24 | open |
~~~

questions.q: Design synthetic monitoring for a banking platform. What journeys do you probe, from where, and how do you avoid false alarms and side effects?
questions.a:
### Why
Real-user signals need traffic; synthetic checks detect failures at 3 a.m. when traffic is low, confirm external reachability (DNS, certificates, CDN), and test critical journeys continuously.

### What to probe
| Probe | Example |
|---|---|
| Availability | public endpoints, login page, API health through the full edge |
| API journeys | authenticate with a test client, get accounts, create and cancel a test payment in a dedicated test account |
| Browser journeys | Playwright: login, view balance, start a transfer (stopping before execution, or against test accounts) |
| Certificates and DNS | expiry, chain, resolution from multiple regions |
| Third parties | payment scheme sandbox or status endpoints |

### Where from
Multiple external locations (regions and ISPs) plus inside the network; compare to separate local issues from global ones.

### Avoiding false alarms and side effects
- Alert only after failures from multiple locations or consecutive runs.
- Dedicated synthetic customers and accounts, excluded from business metrics, fraud models and marketing.
- Mark synthetic traffic with a header and attribute; never move real money.
- Keep test credentials in a vault with rotation.
pts: Detect failures without real traffic.
Probe availability, API and browser journeys, certificates, third parties.
Multiple external locations plus internal.
Alert on multi-location or consecutive failures.
Dedicated synthetic accounts excluded from business data.
questions.ex: An expired intermediate certificate on a CDN broke the mobile API at 2 a.m.; with almost no traffic, real-user alerts didn't fire for hours. Synthetic API journeys from three regions now detect such issues within 5 minutes.
fu: How do you handle MFA in synthetic journeys?
Should synthetics count toward SLOs?
How do you keep synthetics from polluting analytics?

questions.q: On-call engineers receive 150 alerts a week and ignore most. How do you reduce alert fatigue without missing incidents?
questions.a:
### Diagnose
Export a month of alerts: count by rule, how many led to action, how many auto-resolved within minutes, duplicates during the same incident, out-of-hours share.

### Actions
| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| cause-based pages (CPU, memory, restarts) | demote to tickets or dashboards; page on SLO burn |
| flapping alerts | multi-window conditions, {{for}} durations, hysteresis |
| duplicates (10 alerts for one outage) | grouping and inhibition (Alertmanager), dependency-aware alerts |
| no owner | every alert has an owning team label; unowned alerts deleted |
| not actionable | runbook required; if nobody can act, it's not a page |
| noisy thresholds | derive from SLOs or historical baselines, not guesses |
| low-traffic services | longer windows, synthetic probes |

### Process
- Weekly alert review in the on-call handover: every page classified as actionable or not; delete or fix non-actionable ones.
- Targets: for example under 2 pages per on-call shift, over 80% actionable.
- Track on-call health (pages per week, sleep interruptions) as an engineering metric.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Alertmanager: group by incident dimensions and inhibit symptoms of a known upstream failure
route:
  receiver: team-default
  group_by: [team, service, alertname]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
  - matchers: [severity="page"]
    receiver: pagerduty
  - matchers: [severity="ticket"]
    receiver: jira
inhibit_rules:
- source_matchers: [alertname="DatabasePrimaryDown", service="payments-db"]
  target_matchers: [team="payments"]                    # suppress downstream payment symptoms while DB alert is firing
  equal: [region]
~~~
pts: Measure alert actionability first.
Page on symptoms; demote causes.
Group, inhibit and debounce.
Every alert owned with a runbook.
Weekly alert reviews and on-call health targets.
questions.ex: Payments on-call went from 150 alerts a week (8% actionable) to 9 (90% actionable) in two months by converting to SLO burn alerts, grouping, and deleting 60 unowned rules. Mean time to acknowledge real incidents fell from 22 to 4 minutes.
fu: How do you alert on low-traffic services?
What should a runbook contain?
How do you measure on-call health?
pit: Adding alerts after every incident without pruning.

questions.q: How do you observe batch jobs and data pipelines (nightly settlement, statement generation, ETL) where request-based metrics don't apply?
questions.a:
### Signals for batch
| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| **Freshness** | age of the latest successfully processed partition or record; time of last successful run |
| **Completeness** | rows or accounts processed vs expected; missing partitions |
| **Correctness** | reconciliation totals (sum of amounts in vs out), data quality checks (nulls, duplicates, ranges) |
| **Duration and stage timings** | per stage, compared with history |
| **Throughput** | records per second; useful for capacity |
| **Run outcome** | success, partial, failure with reason |

### Alerting
- **Dead-man's switch**: alert if the job did **not** report success by a deadline (absence of a heartbeat).
- SLO on deadline: statements available by 06:00.
- Data-quality failures block downstream steps instead of silently propagating.

### Tracing
One trace per run with spans per stage (long traces: use links between chunk-level traces if needed); correlation id on every record batch.

### Lineage
Track which inputs produced which outputs (lineage tools or run metadata) to answer "which reports used the bad file?".
pts: Freshness, completeness, correctness, duration, outcome.
Dead-man's switch alerts on absence of success.
Deadline SLOs.
Data-quality failures block downstream.
Trace per run; lineage for impact analysis.
questions.ex: A statement job silently processed 92% of accounts for three nights because a partition was missing; no error was raised. Completeness checks against expected account counts and a dead-man's switch now page within minutes of the deadline.
fu: How do you trace a job processing 10 million records?
What data-quality tooling would you use?
How do you handle late-arriving input files?
pit: Only alerting on job failure, not absence.

questions.q: Technical metrics are green but the business reports losses. How do you build business-level observability for a payments platform?
questions.a:
### Business signals
| Signal | Why |
|---|---|
| payments initiated, authorised, settled per minute by scheme and channel | volume anomalies reveal silent failures |
| authorisation approval rate by issuer, scheme, merchant category | drops indicate integration or fraud model issues |
| funnel conversion (start payment to confirmed) | UX or API regressions |
| reconciliation breaks and their value | correctness |
| fee and FX margin per transaction vs tariff | pricing bugs |
| time to settlement | operational SLAs |

### Implementation
- Emit business events (domain events) as metrics with low-cardinality dimensions and as analytics events for deeper slicing.
- **Anomaly detection** on volumes and rates against seasonality (time of day, day of week, month-end): static thresholds fail.
- Business SLOs (approval rate not below baseline minus X) with alerts routed to both engineering and operations.
- Dashboards shared with business operations, with the same definitions as finance reports.

### Ownership
Product and operations co-own business alerts; engineering owns instrumentation.
questions.code:
~~~promql
# Approval rate by scheme vs same hour last week (seasonality-aware comparison)
(
  sum by (scheme) (rate(card_authorisations_total{outcome="approved"}[15m]))
  / sum by (scheme) (rate(card_authorisations_total[15m]))
)
/
(
  sum by (scheme) (rate(card_authorisations_total{outcome="approved"}[15m] offset 1w))
  / sum by (scheme) (rate(card_authorisations_total[15m] offset 1w))
)
< 0.97      # alert when approval rate drops more than 3% relative to last week at this hour
~~~
pts: Track volumes, approval rates, conversion, reconciliation, margins.
Seasonality-aware anomaly detection.
Business SLOs alerting engineering and operations.
Same definitions as finance.
Co-ownership of business alerts.
questions.ex: All technical dashboards were green while a configuration change caused one card scheme's approval rate to drop from 94% to 81% for 6 hours, costing merchants revenue. A seasonality-aware approval-rate alert per scheme caught a similar issue within 15 minutes the next month.
fu: How do you choose comparison baselines?
Metrics or analytics pipeline for business events?
Who is paged for business anomalies?

questions.q: What is continuous profiling, how does eBPF-based observability work, and when are they worth adopting?
questions.a:
### Continuous profiling
Always-on, low-overhead sampling of CPU, allocations, locks and wall time across the fleet, stored as profiles you can query by service, version and time. Answers "which functions got more expensive after the deploy?" without reproducing the issue. Tools: Grafana Pyroscope, Parca, Datadog, Azure Monitor profiler; .NET support via EventPipe-based agents.

### eBPF-based observability
Programs attached in the Linux kernel observe syscalls, network flows and (with symbols) user-space functions without modifying applications:
- Network maps and latency per connection (Cilium Hubble, Pixie).
- Auto-instrumented HTTP and gRPC metrics and traces (Grafana Beyla, OpenTelemetry eBPF instrumentation).
- Profiling.
Limits: kernel version requirements, privileged agents (security review), limited visibility inside encrypted payloads (TLS) unless hooking libraries, managed runtimes (JIT) need runtime support for symbolisation.

### When worth it
Large fleets where CPU cost matters, recurring performance regressions, polyglot estates with uneven instrumentation, or network-level visibility needs. Start with continuous profiling for the most expensive services.
pts: Continuous profiling: always-on CPU, allocation, lock profiles.
Compare profiles across versions.
eBPF observes kernel and network without app changes.
eBPF needs privileged agents and runtime symbol support.
Adopt for large fleets and recurring regressions.
questions.ex: Continuous profiling showed that 18% of a pricing service's CPU after a release went to a regex constructed per request. Caching the compiled regex cut fleet CPU by 15%, saving more than the profiler cost within a month.
fu: What overhead does continuous profiling add?
How do span profiles link traces and profiles?
Security implications of eBPF agents?

questions.q: A SaaS platform serves 2,000 business tenants. How do you observe per-tenant experience and SLOs without exploding cardinality and cost?
questions.a:
### Tension
Per-tenant labels on every metric multiply series by 2,000. Yet support and account managers need "is tenant X having a bad time?".

### Approach
| Tier | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Top tenants (by revenue or contract SLA, maybe 50) | dedicated tenant label on key SLI metrics; per-tenant SLO dashboards and alerts |
| Long tail | aggregated into tiers ({{tier=standard}}); per-tenant analysis via traces and logs (tenant attribute, high-cardinality friendly stores) |
| On demand | temporary per-tenant debug sampling (tail sampling policy keeps all traces for a tenant under investigation) |

### Per-tenant SLIs at scale
Compute per-tenant SLIs from **logs or traces** in a columnar store (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Kusto) rather than as Prometheus series; query hourly or daily for SLA reporting and anomaly detection.

### Isolation of telemetry
If tenants can see their own telemetry (status pages, usage dashboards), enforce tenant filters in queries and never expose other tenants' data.
pts: Per-tenant labels only for top contracted tenants.
Aggregate the long tail by tier.
Per-tenant SLIs from logs or traces in columnar stores.
On-demand tenant debug sampling.
Enforce tenant isolation in shared telemetry views.
questions.ex: Adding tenant_id to all metrics multiplied series by 1,800 and tripled the metrics bill. Moving to top-50 labels plus per-tenant SLIs computed from request logs in ClickHouse kept SLA reporting for all tenants at a fifth of the cost.
fu: How do you alert for long-tail tenants?
How do you expose telemetry to tenants safely?
What is the right columnar store?

questions.q: Audit logs and operational logs are often mixed. Why must they be separate, and how do you design an audit trail for a banking system?
questions.a:
### Different purposes
| Aspect | Operational logs | Audit logs |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | debugging, operations | accountability, compliance, forensics |
| Completeness | sampling acceptable | **must be complete** |
| Retention | days to weeks | years (regulatory) |
| Integrity | best effort | tamper-evident, immutable |
| Access | engineers | restricted: security, audit, compliance |
| Schema | evolving | stable, versioned, defined events |

### Audit event design
Who (authenticated principal, on-behalf-of user, client id), what (action, resource type and id), when (UTC time from a trusted source), where (service, IP, device), outcome (success, denied, error), before and after values where required (or references), correlation id.

### Pipeline
Emitted via a dedicated library and channel (not the general logger), delivered reliably (outbox or durable queue, not best effort), stored in **WORM** storage (immutable blob with legal hold or retention lock) and indexed in the SIEM; hash chaining or signed batches for tamper evidence; access to audit logs is itself audited.

### Typical audited events
Logins and MFA, permission changes, payment approvals, limit changes, data exports, admin actions, configuration changes, break-glass access.
pts: Audit logs must be complete, immutable, long-retained, restricted.
Defined events: who, what, when, where, outcome.
Reliable delivery via outbox, not best-effort logging.
WORM storage and tamper evidence.
Access to audit logs is audited.
questions.ex: A bank sampled all logs at 20% to save cost, including the ones auditors relied on for limit changes; an investigation found gaps. Audit events moved to a dedicated outbox-backed pipeline into WORM storage, never sampled, while operational logs stayed sampled.
fu: How do you prove audit logs weren't altered?
What about PII in audit logs?
How long must they be retained?
pit: Audit events in the general logger.
Engineers with write access to audit stores.

questions.q: How do you observe message-driven systems: consumer lag, processing latency, dead letters and end-to-end flow health?
questions.a:
### Key signals
| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Consumer lag** (messages and **time**) per group and partition | backlog; time lag (age of oldest unconsumed) matters more than counts |
| Processing rate vs produce rate | is the consumer keeping up? |
| Processing duration histogram | per message cost |
| Queue latency (produce to consume) | delay seen by the business |
| Errors, retries, DLQ count and age | poison and failure patterns |
| Rebalances per hour | instability (slow processing, timeouts, deployments) |
| Partition skew | hot partitions limiting parallelism |

### Alerts
Time lag above the flow's SLO (for example payment posting within 60 seconds), DLQ messages present for critical topics, lag growing for N minutes while consumers are healthy (capacity issue).

### Autoscaling
KEDA scaling on lag (bounded by partition count), with alerts when max replicas are reached.

### End-to-end
Business-level freshness: "last settled payment posted to ledger N seconds ago"; trace context through messages (q16).
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# KEDA autoscaling on Kafka lag + alert on time lag (Burrow / exporter metrics)
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: ledger-poster, namespace: ledger }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: ledger-poster }
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 24                 # = partition count
  triggers:
  - type: kafka
    metadata: { bootstrapServers: kafka:9093, consumerGroup: ledger-poster, topic: payments.settled.v1, lagThreshold: "500" }
---
# Prometheus alert on lag measured in time
# - alert: LedgerPostingLagHigh
#   expr: max(kafka_consumergroup_lag_seconds{group="ledger-poster"}) > 60
#   for: 5m
#   labels: { severity: page, team: ledger }
~~~
pts: Lag in time matters more than message counts.
Compare processing and produce rates.
Track DLQ, retries, rebalances, partition skew.
Alert on time lag vs flow SLO.
Autoscale on lag up to partition count.
questions.ex: Lag in messages looked fine (2,000) but those were 6 minutes of payments during a quiet period; statement balances were stale. Alerting on time lag with a 60-second SLO caught slow posting during the next low-volume night.
fu: How do you measure time lag?
What causes frequent rebalances?
How do you observe Service Bus queues?

questions.q: How do you manage dashboards, alerts, SLOs and collector configuration as code, and what does that enable?
questions.a:
### What goes in Git
- Collector configuration (Helm values), with validation in CI.
- Alert rules (Prometheus rule files, vendor monitors via Terraform providers).
- SLO definitions (OpenSLO, Sloth, vendor resources) generating recording rules and burn-rate alerts.
- Dashboards (Grafonnet or Jsonnet, Terraform), generated from templates per service.
- Runbooks next to alert definitions.

### Workflow
PRs with review by the owning team; CI checks: syntax (promtool, amtool), unit tests for alert rules ({{promtool test rules}}), lint (every alert has team, severity, runbook), dry-run against the backend.

### What it enables
- New services get standard dashboards and SLO alerts automatically from the service catalogue.
- Consistency across teams; history of changes (who changed the threshold and why).
- Recreating the observability setup in another region or vendor.
- Preventing "click-ops" drift.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Sloth SLO spec generates recording rules and multi-window burn-rate alerts
version: prometheus/v1
service: payments-api
labels: { team: payments }
slos:
  - name: availability
    objective: 99.95
    description: "Gateway-measured availability for payments routes"
    sli:
      events:
        error_query: sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*",code=~"5.."}[{{.window}}]))
        total_query: sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route=~"/payments.*",code!~"4.."}[{{.window}}]))
    alerting:
      name: PaymentsAvailability
      page_alert: { labels: { severity: page } }
      ticket_alert: { labels: { severity: ticket } }
      annotations: { runbook: https://runbooks.bank/payments/availability }
---
# promtool rule unit test (CI)
# promtool test rules tests/payments-alerts.test.yml
~~~
pts: Collector config, alerts, SLOs, dashboards, runbooks in Git.
Review, validate and unit-test alert rules.
Generate standard assets per service.
History and consistency across teams.
Reproducible setup; no click-ops drift.
questions.ex: A critical alert was silently disabled in a UI by someone silencing noise; nobody noticed until an outage went undetected. With alerts as code and CI lint, changes require review and disabling a page alert needs an explicit, approved PR.
fu: How do you test alert rules?
Sloth vs vendor SLO features?
How do you handle UI experimentation?

questions.q: Many incidents start at third parties (payment schemes, KYC providers, cloud services). How do you observe dependencies you don't control?
questions.a:
### Client-side telemetry
Every outbound call instrumented: latency histograms, error rates by error class (timeouts, 4xx, 5xx, TLS), retries and circuit breaker state, **per provider and per endpoint**. This is your source of truth when the vendor's status page says "all green".

### Additional signals
- Synthetic probes to provider sandbox or health endpoints.
- Provider status pages and webhooks ingested as events.
- Business outcome metrics per provider (approval rates, verification pass rates).
- Contractual SLA tracking: measure their availability as you experience it, for credits and vendor reviews.

### Resilience visibility
Dashboard shows fallback usage (cached data, secondary provider), queue backlogs for deferred work, and degraded-mode indicators.

### Correlation
Pass and log the provider's request ids (and send your correlation id if supported) so joint investigations are fast; agree on incident contacts and escalation paths in the contract.
pts: Instrument every outbound call per provider and endpoint.
Your client view beats vendor status pages.
Synthetic probes and business outcomes per provider.
Track experienced SLAs for vendor management.
Log provider request ids for joint debugging.
questions.ex: A KYC provider's status page stayed green during a 3-hour degradation; the bank's client-side histograms showed p99 at 14 seconds and timeouts at 30%. The data supported a fallback activation and later an SLA credit claim.
fu: How do you measure a vendor's SLA fairly?
What fallback strategies exist for KYC?
How do you get vendors to propagate trace ids?
pit: No provider request ids in logs.

questions.q: What Kubernetes-level telemetry do you need beyond application metrics, and which common platform problems does it reveal?
questions.a:
### Telemetry
| Source | Signals |
|---|---|
| kube-state-metrics | deployment replicas, pod phases, restarts, HPA status, PVC status |
| cAdvisor / kubelet | container CPU, memory, **CPU throttling** ({{container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total}}), OOM kills |
| Kubernetes events | scheduling failures, evictions, image pull errors, probe failures |
| Node metrics | pressure conditions, disk, network, conntrack table |
| Control plane | API server latency and errors, etcd health (managed clusters expose some) |
| Cluster autoscaler / Karpenter | pending pods, scale-up latency |

### Problems revealed
- **CPU throttling** from low CPU limits: latency spikes with low average CPU (a classic .NET issue when limits are below the GC and thread pool's needs).
- OOM kills from limits too low or leaks.
- Pending pods from insufficient capacity or affinity rules.
- Probe misconfiguration causing restarts under load.
- Noisy neighbours on shared nodes.
- DNS latency (CoreDNS saturation, ndots) causing slow outbound calls.

### Practice
Correlate platform events with service dashboards (restart and throttling panels on every service dashboard).
questions.code:
~~~promql
# CPU throttling ratio per container (latency spikes despite low average CPU)
sum by (namespace, pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="payments"}[5m]))
  / sum by (namespace, pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="payments"}[5m]))
> 0.25

# OOM kills in the last hour
increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="payments"}[1h]) > 0
  and on (namespace, pod, container) kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"} == 1

# Pods pending for more than 5 minutes
max by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Pending"}) == 1
~~~
pts: kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor, events, nodes, control plane, autoscaler.
CPU throttling causes latency with low average CPU.
OOM kills, pending pods, probe restarts.
DNS saturation slows outbound calls.
Show restarts and throttling on service dashboards.
questions.ex: A payments API had p99 spikes every few seconds with 30% average CPU; throttling metrics showed 60% of periods throttled under a 500m CPU limit. Raising the limit (and setting GC heap limits appropriately) removed the spikes.
fu: Should you set CPU limits at all?
How do you observe CoreDNS?
What events matter most?

questions.q: Design an observability platform for 500 services across 4 regions: ingestion, storage, querying, multi-tenancy and reliability.
questions.a:
### Ingestion
OpenTelemetry SDKs in apps, collector agents per node, regional collector gateways (tail sampling, redaction, routing), with persistent queues; Kafka as a buffer for logs at very high volume.

### Storage (example open-source stack; vendors map similarly)
| Signal | Store | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics | Mimir or Thanos (Prometheus-compatible, object storage) | per-tenant limits on series |
| Logs | Loki or a columnar store (ClickHouse) | label discipline; object storage |
| Traces | Tempo or Jaeger with object storage | tail-sampled |
| Profiles | Pyroscope | |
| SLOs and alerts | Prometheus-compatible rulers, Alertmanager | per-team routing |

### Regional design
Data stays in-region (residency, egress cost); global query federation for cross-region views; alerting evaluated regionally so a region's monitoring doesn't depend on another region.

### Multi-tenancy
Tenant = team or domain: quotas (ingest rate, series), access control, cost showback.

### Reliability of the platform
The observability platform must be **more** reliable than what it observes and independent of it (separate clusters, out-of-band alerting path, a minimal external monitor of the monitoring). SLOs for the platform itself (ingestion delay, query latency, alert evaluation).

flowchart LR
  subgraph Region[Each region]
    APPS[Services - OTel SDK] --> AG[Collector agents]
    AG --> GW[Collector gateways: sample, redact, route]
    GW --> MIM[(Metrics - Mimir)]
    GW --> LOK[(Logs - Loki)]
    GW --> TMP[(Traces - Tempo)]
    MIM --> RUL[Rulers and Alertmanager]
  end
  RUL --> PAGE[Paging]
  MIM --> GQ[Global query federation]

~~~yaml
# Mimir per-tenant limits (tenant = team) protect the shared platform
overrides:
  team-payments:
    ingestion_rate: 400000           # samples per second
    max_global_series_per_user: 3000000
    max_label_names_per_series: 30
    ruler_max_rules_per_rule_group: 50
  team-marketing:
    ingestion_rate: 50000
    max_global_series_per_user: 300000
---
# Out-of-band dead man's switch: Alertmanager sends a heartbeat every minute to an external service;
# if heartbeats stop, the external service pages via a separate provider.
- alert: Watchdog
  expr: vector(1)
  labels: { severity: heartbeat }
~~~
pts: OTel SDKs, agents, regional gateways, persistent queues.
Object-storage-backed metrics, logs, traces, profiles.
Regional data and alerting; global query federation.
Per-team tenancy with quotas and showback.
Platform more reliable than workloads, with external watchdogs.
questions.ex: A bank's single global monitoring cluster went down with the region it lived in, leaving all regions blind during the outage. Regional stacks with an external watchdog meant the next regional failure was visible from the other regions immediately.

How do you migrate between backends?
What are the platform's own SLOs?

questions.q: Observability now costs more than the infrastructure it observes. How do you bring it under control without losing incident capability?
questions.a:
### Understand
Cost breakdown by signal, team and source; usage data (which dashboards, queries and alerts are used; which logs are ever read).

### Levers
| Lever | Typical saving |
|---|---|
| Logs: remove per-request info logs duplicated by traces, drop noise, sample info, tiered retention | 30 to 60% of log cost |
| Metrics: cardinality budgets, drop unused metrics (usage analysis), aggregate before storage | 20 to 50% |
| Traces: tail sampling, drop health checks, shorter retention for baseline traces | 40 to 70% |
| Retention by purpose: hot 7 to 14 days, archive cheap | storage |
| Vendor pricing: commit discounts, moving bulk logs to cheaper stores, OSS for high-volume signals | large |
| Showback and team budgets | behaviour change |

### Guardrails
Keep: errors and warnings, SLO metrics, audit and security logs (separate pipelines), tail-sampled error and slow traces. Validate with incident replays ("could we have diagnosed the last five incidents with the reduced data?").

### Governance
Telemetry budget per team (for example a percentage of their infrastructure cost), quarterly reviews, platform defaults that are cost-efficient (golden-path instrumentation).
questions.code:
~~~sql
-- Which metrics are never queried? (from backend query logs over 30 days)
SELECT m.metric_name, m.active_series, COALESCE(q.queries_30d, 0) AS queries_30d
FROM metric_inventory m
LEFT JOIN (SELECT metric_name, COUNT(*) AS queries_30d FROM query_log WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL 30 DAY GROUP BY metric_name) q
  ON q.metric_name = m.metric_name
WHERE COALESCE(q.queries_30d, 0) = 0 AND m.metric_name NOT IN (SELECT metric FROM alert_rule_metrics)
ORDER BY m.active_series DESC
LIMIT 50;   -- candidates to drop at the collector
~~~
pts: Break down cost by signal, team and source.
Usage analysis finds unused metrics and logs.
Fix at source, sample, tier retention, cardinality budgets.
Keep errors, SLO data, audit and tail-sampled traces.
Validate cuts with incident replays; team budgets.
questions.ex: An observability bill of 4.2M a year exceeded the cloud compute bill. Usage analysis showed 41% of metric series and 55% of log volume were never queried; after removal, sampling and tiering, cost fell to 1.9M and an incident-replay review confirmed no diagnostic gaps.

OSS vs vendor at this scale?
How do you prevent cost creeping back?

questions.q: Write the decision between a commercial observability vendor and a self-hosted open-source stack (Grafana LGTM). What criteria decide it, and how do you avoid lock-in either way?
questions.a:
### Criteria
| Criterion | Vendor (Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, Elastic Cloud, Grafana Cloud) | Self-hosted OSS |
|---|---|---|
| Time to value | fast | slower; platform build |
| Features (APM, RUM, profiling, AIOps, security) | broad, integrated | assemble; gaps |
| Cost at scale | often high, usage-based, hard to predict | infrastructure plus engineers; cheaper at very high volume |
| Operations | vendor runs it | you run, scale, upgrade it (team of several engineers) |
| Data residency and control | depends on regions offered | full control |
| Lock-in | proprietary agents and query languages | open formats |
| Skills | lower | needs SRE capability |

### Avoiding lock-in
- OpenTelemetry SDKs and collectors everywhere (no proprietary agents in code).
- Dashboards and alerts as code with an abstraction layer where possible (SLO specs).
- Dual-export during evaluations and migrations.
- Contracts with data export rights and exit clauses.

### Common outcome
Hybrid: vendor for APM, RUM and traces where features matter; OSS or cheaper stores for bulk logs and long retention metrics; OTel as the neutral layer.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# ADR-070: Observability backend strategy
status: accepted
date: 2026-10-13
decision:
  instrumentation: OpenTelemetry SDKs and Collector only (no proprietary agents)
  traces_rum_profiling: vendor (EU region), tail-sampled at our gateway
  metrics: self-hosted Mimir (object storage), vendor receives SLO metrics only
  logs: self-hosted Loki for operational logs (14d hot, 12m archive); audit logs to WORM + SIEM
drivers:
  - vendor log ingestion projected at 3.1M/year vs 0.9M self-hosted incl. 3 FTE
  - APM features needed by 40 teams immediately
  - EU residency for all telemetry
exit:
  - collector config switch to alternative backend; dashboards as Grafonnet
  - contract: full data export, 90-day exit assistance
review: annually or on 25 percent cost deviation
~~~
pts: Vendor: fast, broad, costly at scale.
OSS: control and cost at scale, needs a platform team.
OpenTelemetry everywhere avoids lock-in.
Dashboards and alerts as code; dual export.
Hybrid is common.

questions.q: Roll out an SLO practice across 60 teams that currently use only uptime checks. How do you make it stick?
questions.a:
### Start with journeys
Identify the top customer journeys (login, view balance, pay, onboard) with product owners; define SLIs at the edge or client for each; set initial SLOs from historical data (slightly better than current reality, not aspirational).

### Enable teams
- SLO tooling as a platform service: SLO specs in Git generate recording rules, burn-rate alerts and dashboards.
- Templates and examples per service type (API, consumer, batch).
- Training: what SLIs are, how to choose targets, how to use budgets.

### Make it matter
- Error budget policies agreed with product leadership.
- Monthly service reviews looking at SLO performance and budget spend, not raw incident counts.
- Paging moves from cause alerts to SLO burn alerts.
- Use SLOs in planning: teams with exhausted budgets prioritise reliability work.

### Avoid
Hundreds of SLOs nobody reviews; SLOs on internal components with no user meaning; targets copied from Google; punishing teams for missing SLOs (they will set targets they can't miss).

### Measure adoption
Percentage of critical journeys with SLOs, alerts derived from SLOs, budget policies in use, incidents detected by SLO alerts first.

# Journey SLO catalogue (owned jointly by product and engineering)
journeys:
  - name: make-payment
    owner: { product: payments-po, engineering: team-payments }
    sli: gateway-measured success and latency for POST /payments and confirmation
    slos: [{ type: availability, target: 99.95 }, { type: latency, threshold_ms: 800, target: 99.0 }]
    error_budget_policy: policies/payments.md
    review: monthly-service-review
  - name: view-balance
    owner: { product: accounts-po, engineering: team-accounts }
    sli: RUM - balance tile rendered within 2s after login
    slos: [{ type: latency, threshold_ms: 2000, target: 98.5 }]
adoption:
  critical_journeys_with_slo: 14/16
  pages_from_slo_alerts_pct: 72
~~~

Platform tooling turns SLO specs into alerts and dashboards.
Budget policies agreed with product.
Monthly reviews; planning uses budgets.
Measure adoption; never punish misses.

questions.q: Teams name metrics and attributes inconsistently, so cross-service queries are impossible. Define observability standards and enforce them without slowing teams.
questions.a:
### Standards
1. **OpenTelemetry semantic conventions** as the baseline (http, db, messaging, rpc, exceptions) and resource attributes ({{service.name}}, {{service.version}}, {{deployment.environment.name}}, {{cloud.region}}, {{k8s.*}}).
2. **Organisation conventions** for domain attributes with a namespace ({{bank.tenant}}, {{bank.channel}}, {{bank.payment.scheme}}), documented in a registry with allowed values and cardinality class.
3. Naming rules for custom metrics ({{bank.payments.created}}), units, histogram buckets for latency classes.
4. Logging: structured, event ids per message template, levels policy, correlation ids, PII rules.
5. Required signals per service archetype: RED metrics, traces with propagation, SLO definitions, runbooks.

### Enforcement with low friction
- **Shared instrumentation package** ({{Bank.Telemetry}}) configuring OpenTelemetry with the standards by default; teams add one line.
- Collector processors normalise or drop non-conforming attributes.
- CI checks (lint metric names in code, alert rule linting).
- Scorecards per service (conformance percentage) in the developer portal.

### Evolution
Versioned conventions with migration notes; semantic convention stability changes in OpenTelemetry tracked by the platform team.
pts: OTel semantic conventions plus namespaced org attributes.
Registry of attributes with cardinality class.
Shared instrumentation package applies standards by default.
Collector normalisation, CI lint, scorecards.
Versioned conventions with migration notes.
questions.ex: Three teams named the same latency metric differently in different units; an incident review couldn't compare them. A shared Bank.Telemetry package and an attribute registry made all new services conform automatically and the collector renamed legacy metrics during migration.

What goes in the attribute registry?
